case_study_insert.main_stem: Brightwood Nursery Group (BNG) is a private limited company in the early-years education sector, employing a workforce of 132. Founded in 2011 by Hannah Whitmore, BNG operates three nursery and preschool sites across the Brightwood region and uses a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. It plans to invest $750,000 in a fourth nursery in Riverside and gain national early-years quality accreditation, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $528,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. BNG faces difficult recruitment of qualified childcare practitioners, staff turnover of 27%, and a waiting list of 145 children.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The three sites delivered 22,500 nursery session units last quarter at an incident rate of 0.9%, down from 1.7% a year ago. Parent complaints fell from 26 to 14 per month. A survey of 800 parents found 71% rated staff friendliness excellent and 57% want the Riverside site to offer forest-school sessions; 44% would pay up to $14 more per week for places. Off-the-job training at the local college costs $820 per practitioner. A waiting list of 145 children covers all three sites, and 33 of 132 staff are on fixed-term contracts.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Brightwood Nursery Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.15 to $13.01 per hour from April 2026, raising childcare wage bills. (3) Nursery consumables and food costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, education-services inflation is running at 6.5%, and consumer spending on early-years places grew 4.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: BNG plans to finance part of its Riverside expansion and accreditation bid with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for BNG of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs BNG nothing in interest or arrangement fees, protecting its cash flow at a time when it already carries fixed costs of $528,000 a year and a proposed $450,000 ten-year bank loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 10.8% rise in consumables and food costs and helps BNG keep its $16.50 average session price accessible while it bids for national early-years quality accreditation and fills Riverside places amid a waiting list of 145 children.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk of borrowing against the new $750,000 Riverside nursery, so the $300,000 stays available without risking the site if occupancy starts slowly or consumer spending growth of 4.6% stalls. It also preserves Hannah Whitmore's ownership and control, since no lender can dictate staffing ratios, the curriculum mix such as the forest-school sessions wanted by 57% of surveyed parents, or the pace at which BNG integrates the fourth site.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Brightwood Nursery Group, its Riverside expansion and its accreditation bid.

questions.question_text: BNG is promoting the opening of its Riverside nursery and its accreditation bid. Consider a regional television campaign, local radio advertising, or targeted social media advertising aimed at parents. Which should BNG choose to promote the new nursery? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television campaign: A regional TV campaign would build strong brand awareness for the Brightwood name quickly and reassure parents considering early-years places, especially couples not yet researching nurseries. However, production and airtime costs are extremely high and much of the audience has no preschool-age children, so wastage is large for a 132-employee group funding a $750,000 expansion and a $450,000 bank loan.

Local radio advertising: Local radio is far cheaper than television, reaches Brightwood and Riverside parents on school runs and commuting routes, and suits time-sensitive messages such as an opening week offer or accreditation news. However, reach is narrow and listener attention is fragmented; the Riverside site aims to serve a wide area with a 145-child waiting list, so radio alone cannot convert awareness into enough enrolments fast enough to cover fixed costs of $528,000 a year.

Targeted social media advertising: Social media lets BNG aim ads precisely at parents of under-fives in the Riverside catchment, show the 71% staff-friendliness rating, promote the forest-school sessions wanted by 57% of 800 surveyed parents and retarget visitors to the booking page. It is measurable, scalable and reinforces the accreditation story at a fraction of TV cost, though results depend on good creative and prompt responses to parent messages.

Recommendation: BNG should choose targeted social media advertising. It reaches exactly the parent segment identified in its research, costs far less than television, scales beyond radio's narrow regional reach, and evidences the accreditation-seeking, child-centred positioning behind Riverside. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 132-employee group; local radio is rejected as too narrow to fill a fourth nursery on its own — it can play a supporting role, not the lead.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of BNG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of BNG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: BNG's staff turnover has reached 27%. Explain two benefits for BNG of using democratic leadership to improve motivation in its childcare teams.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 132 practitioners to help shape session planning, ratios, rota design and the Riverside curriculum rather than simply receiving instructions. Giving staff a voice raises job satisfaction and meets social and esteem needs, reducing the frustration behind 27% turnover and helping BNG hold the practitioners parents rate so highly (71% friendliness), which is vital while difficult recruitment stretches teams across three sites and a waiting list of 145 children.

Point 2: Involving staff generates practical ideas from those who deliver 22,500 nursery session units last quarter at a 0.9% incident rate, down from 1.7%. Suggestion-driven tweaks to forest-school delivery (wanted by 57% of parents), risk routines and fixed-term contract handling for the 33 staff affected could cut turnover further, reduce recruitment and retraining costs, and protect output of 90,000 units a year while the fourth nursery staffs up; staff who helped design the Riverside plan will also brief new joiners, making onboarding smoother for an expanding group.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BNG's turnover, incident rate, waiting list and output.

questions.question_text: BNG must train its practitioners on the new forest-school curriculum wanted by Riverside parents. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should BNG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside experienced practitioners on site is directly relevant to BNG's own outdoor settings, risk assessments and forest-school routines, costs no tuition fees and keeps practitioners productive with the 145-child waiting list to serve across three sites. However, it depends on mentor availability, can pass on inconsistent practice if supervision is stretched by 27% turnover, and gives no external certificate — a real weakness when the national early-years quality accreditation bid needs externally verified competence to satisfy inspectors.

Off-the-job training at the local college: College courses at $820 per practitioner give structured, up-to-date forest-school skills and formal certificates, an insert-costed $820 per practitioner that BNG can multiply by however many practitioners it enrols, modest against a $750,000 expansion and a $450,000 bank loan commitment. However, staff are removed from the sites for days at a time, ratios must be covered by agency or overtime at extra cost, content is generic rather than matched to BNG's grounds, and travel plus back-fill add strain for an already stretched workforce of 132. Scheduling can also clash with peak admissions periods.

Decision: BNG should choose off-the-job training at the local college for its lead practitioners, combined with short on-the-job coaching afterwards. The accreditation bid demands externally verified competence and the certificates strengthen it; on-the-job-only delivery is rejected because inconsistent forest-school practice would undermine safety, the accreditation audit and the 57% parental demand for these sessions. The $820 per practitioner cost is small against the $750,000 investment, avoids agency cover overruns, and builds a certified base on which on-site coaching can then layer, protecting the 0.9% incident rate the sites have worked to achieve.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to BNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of BNG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of BNG with a well-justified decision tied to accreditation, ratios, waiting lists and cost.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how BNG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $528,000 ÷ ($16.50 − $9.00) = $528,000 ÷ $7.50 = 70,400 units. Answer: break-even output is 70,400 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.50 − $9.00 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways BNG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 70,400-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units to confirm the three sites are profitable with a margin of safety of 19,600 units, informing how quickly the Riverside site can reach break-even.
2. Use contribution per unit of $7.50 to test fee changes or subsidies, for example a 6% sibling discount to $15.51 would cut contribution to $6.51, letting managers judge whether the 145-child waiting list converts into enough funded places at Riverside.
3. Check the $450,000 ten-year bank loan is serviceable by verifying the 19,600-unit margin of safety survives fee pressure and the 10.8% rise in food and consumables before committing to the $750,000 Riverside investment.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($528,000 ÷ 90,000 units + $9.00 = $14.87 a unit) across sites to spot the weakest performing site, challenge the 0.9% incident rate and tighten purchasing before the accreditation inspection.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 70,400 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 19,600 units against 90,000-unit output; discount and subsidy modelling against the $528,000 fixed costs; feasibility checking for the $450,000 bank loan funding Riverside; unit-cost benchmarking at $14.87 to drive the accreditation bid and cut the 0.9% incident rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate BNG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has BNG's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 20.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $455,000 on revenue $1,300,000 (cost of sales $845,000); 2025 gross profit $594,000 on revenue $1,485,000 (cost of sales $891,000). 2024 operating profit $195,000; 2025 operating profit $297,000. 2024 capital employed $1,560,000; 2025 capital employed $1,980,000. Interest payable rose from $22,000 to $30,000; the extract records the increase but does not give its cause.

Evaluation: Underlying performance improved solidly. Gross profit grew from $455,000 to $594,000 (30.5%) as revenue rose $185,000 and cost of sales as a share of revenue fell from 65.0% to 60.0% — helped by the incident rate falling from 1.7% to 0.9% and complaints from 26 to 14 per month. Operating profit grew from $195,000 to $297,000 (52.3%), well ahead of revenue growth of 14.2%, so overheads and accreditation-readiness spending were absorbed efficiently. Capital employed rose from $1,560,000 to $1,980,000, yet the return on that capital still strengthened. However, consumable-cost inflation of 10.8% and any occupancy shortfall at Riverside could erode these gains, and fixed-term contracts for 33 staff need renewal planning.

Conclusion: Yes, BNG's financial performance has improved. Revenue, gross profit and operating profit all grew, cost discipline genuinely improved and the return on capital employed climbed from 12.5% to 15.0%. The judgement is not risk-free — interest charges are rising and consumables are inflating — so BNG should secure Riverside enrolments early, progress the accreditation bid and keep tight control of meal and consumable purchasing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, interest and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether BNG's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for BNG of offering forest-school sessions at its Riverside site.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Forest-school sessions respond directly to the 57% of the 800 surveyed parents who want them, letting Riverside stand out from nearby nurseries and supporting a premium — 44% of parents would pay up to $14 more per week for places, which protects the $7.50 contribution per unit while consumables inflate 10.8%. The distinctive offer strengthens the national early-years quality accreditation bid, helps fill Riverside places quickly against the 145-child waiting list and lifts occupancy well above the level needed to service the $450,000 bank loan.

Disadvantage: Outdoor forest-school delivery carries higher supervision, risk-assessment, clothing and equipment costs, which raise the $9.00 variable cost per unit and may compress the advantage if the $14 premium is not paid consistently. Staff need extra training ($820 per practitioner), incidents could damage the 0.9% incident-rate record and any accreditation failure would waste the $750,000 spent on the Riverside site and delay its route to profitability.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to BNG's parent research, costs and accreditation bid.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in consumables and food costs will affect BNG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If BNG's planned $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, a 0.75 percentage point increase adds about $3,375 a year (0.75% × $450,000) of extra interest, lifting BNG's financing cost; the extract shows interest payable of $30,000 in 2025 but does not state the loan's rate structure, so this impact is conditional. Higher rates also make the remaining funding need for the $750,000 Riverside nursery costlier and could dampen consumer willingness to fund paid places; BNG can negotiate to fix the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.01 per hour): The rise is $0.86 an hour ($13.01 − $12.15) on every minimum-wage hour worked. BNG employs 132 staff, and early-years delivery is labour-intensive, so the increase touches every practitioner paid at or near the minimum, as well as any agency cover brought in while 33 staff are on fixed-term contracts. The insert contains no wage-bill total or hours worked, so the exact annual cost cannot be quantified from the figures provided; what is certain is that it is permanent, recurs hourly, and lands at the same time as difficult recruitment of qualified practitioners and 27% turnover.

Input cost inflation (10.8% consumables and food): Nursery consumables and food costs — a major element of the $9.00 variable cost per unit — have risen 10.8% year-on-year. Across 90,000 units the variable-cost spend pools to $810,000 ($9.00 × 90,000, computable from the insert). The extract does not split consumables from other variable costs, so the precise annual impact cannot be computed, but a 10.8% rise raises the cost of every session and threatens the fall in cost of sales as a share of revenue from 65.0% to 60.0% that drove gross profit from $455,000 to $594,000 — the gain underpinning the accreditation story parents were shown.

Conclusion: The 7.1% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest rise — quantifiable at about $3,375 a year on the planned $450,000 loan even if it is variable-rate — and unlike the consumables rise, whose share of the $810,000 variable-cost pool is not given in the insert, the wage rise recurs on every hour of the labour-intensive early-years workforce, raising recruitment and retention costs precisely when recruitment is difficult and 27% turnover persists. It also squeezes the occupancy-led profit BNG needs to service the $450,000 loan. Consumable inflation is the second most serious risk; the interest rise is the smallest quantifiable impact and can be fixed, but both still demand tighter rota planning, fee reviews and occupancy discipline.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to BNG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on BNG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of BNG with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact, and why the consumables rise and the interest rise are smaller.
